I have taken small groups on ten-day trips for about fifteen years, and I want to tell you the one thing that separates the people who enjoy a trip from the people who survive it. It is not money, it is not the hotel, and it is honestly not the language either. On a ten-day trip, something goes wrong roughly four times. A bag arrives late. A room is not ready at two in the afternoon. Somebody tells you the wrong time for something. And there is always one line on a bill that nobody explained. Four hiccups, and none of them is a disaster. What changes everything is the first thirty seconds after each one. Some people wait. They stand near the desk hoping that somebody notices them, and by the time they speak, the person who could have fixed it has gone home. Other people walk up, say what happened, say what they need, and go back to their holiday. Those two groups had exactly the same trip. Only one of them remembers it as a good one. And here is the part people do not believe until it happens to them: your English does not have to be good for the second version. It has to be quick.

I work the front desk of a hotel in Miami Beach, and the last morning is the one guests always get wrong, so let me save you an hour of your life. First, check out is at eleven, but your bags do not have to leave when you do. We store them for free until the evening, and almost nobody asks, so people carry a suitcase around the city on their last day for no reason at all. Second, ask for the final bill the night before, not on the morning itself, because that is when you have time to read it and ask about the line you do not recognise. Every hotel bill in this country has one, and it is almost always a fee that is perfectly normal once somebody explains it. Third, and this is the one I would write on the door if they let me, tell us the night before what time your flight is. If we know, we book the shuttle, we hold a late room for you to change in, and we have the bags at the door when you come back. If we do not know, we cannot do any of it. It takes one sentence at the desk, and it is the difference between a calm last day and a bad one.
